entities.name: Fatih Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Fatih Mosque (Mosque of the Conqueror) in Istanbul is one of the most important mosques in Turkey, built by Sultan Mehmed II (the Conqueror) after his conquest of Constantinople in 1453 CE. The original mosque, completed in 1470 CE, was built on the site of the Byzantine Church of the Holy Apostles — the burial church of Byzantine emperors and second most important church in Christendom after Hagia Sophia — creating a powerful statement of Ottoman succession to Byzantine empire.

Mehmed II's choice of the Church of the Holy Apostles site was deliberate: the Apostoleion was where Constantine I and Byzantine emperors were buried, where the relics of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy were kept, and which Constantine himself had built as his mausoleum. By replacing this imperial Christian structure with a mosque, Mehmed symbolically completed the Islamic succession to Roman imperial power. The original mosque was destroyed in the 1766 earthquake; the current building is an 18th-century replacement.

The Fatih complex (külliye) was among the most ambitious social complexes in Ottoman history: eight madrasas, a hospital, library, caravanserai, public baths, and the mosque formed a comprehensive educational and social welfare system. The complex produced graduates who became the Ottoman religious and intellectual elite. Mehmed II's own tomb, in the mosque garden, is one of Istanbul's most-visited Ottoman imperial shrines.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Fatih Mosque's construction on the Byzantine imperial church site is one of history's most powerful symbolic acts of imperial succession, marking Constantinople's transformation from Christian to Islamic capital.
